articles.title: Simple Box-Cox probabilistic models for hourly streamflow predictions
articles.titleEn: Simple Box-Cox probabilistic models for hourly streamflow predictions
articles.abstract: The increasing availability of hourly scale hydrological data offers valuable benefits for advancing our understanding of catchment processes and improving prediction capabilities. This work contributes to streamflow predictions at the hourly scale by investigating practical methods for uncertainty quantification using probabilistic models. We examine common approaches for representing the heteroscedasticity of streamflow errors using the Box-Cox (BC) transformation and common approaches for representing the autocorrelation of streamflow errors using autoregressive (AR) models. Case studies based on 7 catchments from Spain, Switzerland and USA that cover humid to semi-arid conditions are reported. The results favor Box-Cox transformations with power parameter values of 0–0.5. Notably the Log transformation achieves the best statistical reliability of predictions, while its precision and volumetric bias are not statistically significantly worse than for other transformations considered in this study. Catchment-by-catchment variability becomes more pronounced when performance is stratified to the top 5 % of flows. The results also tend to favor the AR2 and AR3 models over the AR1 model for representing the error autocorrelation, with the addition of moving average terms generally providing little additional benefit. Our findings are broadly consistent with earlier work with daily data, and provide practical guidance for hydrologists and practitioners requiring uncertainty quantification at the hourly scale. We also report progress towards “seamless” aggregation from hourly to longer scales, which is a capability that is desirable in many practical operational contexts.

articles.title: Climatology of the sea temperature from long-term in situ observations: Northern Chilean Patagonia
articles.titleEn: Climatology of the sea temperature from long-term in situ observations: Northern Chilean Patagonia
articles.abstract: Ocean climatologies are essential for understanding the mean state and variability of marine systems, providing reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning and identifying long-term trends. In this study, we present the first high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia, a region characterised by the presence of a complex network of fjords and channels. The climatology was generated from approximately three million in situ observations collected over the past 75 years from multiple datasets. Using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis in n dimensions (DIVAnd) tool, temperature fields were reconstructed with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertical levels, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth. The resulting climatology accurately reproduces the main spatial and seasonal temperature patterns reported in previous studies. Surface temperatures show strong summer gradients between the open Pacific and Northern Patagonia, while enclosed regions such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords exhibit pronounced seasonal amplitude compared with more stable basins such as Corcovado Gulf. Below surface, temperature gradients become smoother and the thermocline deepens in summer, typically ranging between 10 and 50 m. At 100 m depth, temperatures are relatively constant throughout the year, but spatial variations are still observed, with Ancud Gulf and Reloncaví Sound being slightly warmer. In addition, a daily-derived climatology for the upper 100 m (14 depth levels) was generated from the monthly fields using temporal interpolation and smoothing, in order to support applications requiring daily temporal resolution. These temperature climatologies provide a refined and physically consistent representation of the oceanographic structures of Northern Patagonia, offering an essential baseline for future modelling, monitoring and climate-change assessments in a region where satellite observations are limited by persistent cloud cover and complex topography. All climatologies generated in this study are freely available online as NetCDF3-Classic datasets (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21959707, Pujol et al., 2026).

articles.title: Protected Areas Reduce Heat Exposure in Squamates Globally
articles.titleEn: Protected Areas Reduce Heat Exposure in Squamates Globally
articles.abstract: Protected areas (PAs) are central to biodiversity conservation, yet their capacity to buffer species from climate‐driven heat exposure, that is, the duration and frequency of exposure to temperatures exceeding species' critical thermal limits, remains poorly quantified at global scales. Here, we assessed whether squamate reptiles inside PAs experience lower heat exposure than conspecifics in unprotected, human‐modified landscapes, and how this buffering effect varies across latitudes, biomes, and evolutionary lineages. Using biophysical modelling of operative temperatures across 248 species, we show that PAs consistently reduced both annual hours above critical thermal maximum (CT max ) and the frequency of critical days under current and future climatic scenarios (+2°C and + 4°C). We found that under current climate, protected sites had 51 fewer hours above CT max and 3.5 fewer critical days than unprotected sites, and the proportional reduction persisted under +2°C and + 4°C warming scenarios. The buffering effect was most pronounced at low latitudes and tropical biomes, where species already operate close to their thermal limits. Deserts and xeric shrublands, together with tropical grasslands and savannas, emerged as biomes with elevated heat exposure, reinforcing growing concern for arid‐zone reptiles under climate change. Substantial phylogenetic signal in heat exposure indicated that evolutionary history shapes thermal vulnerability beyond geography and biome alone, with the magnitude of PA buffering varying considerably across squamate lineages. Our findings demonstrate that PAs can provide refugia from heat exposure, and that their conservation value under climate change depends on the retention of structurally complex habitats and thermally heterogeneous microhabitats.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Optimize Ecological Restoration for Climate and Biodiversity
articles.titleEn: Using Artificial Intelligence to Optimize Ecological Restoration for Climate and Biodiversity
articles.abstract: The restoration of degraded ecosystems is critical for mitigating climate change and reversing biodiversity loss. Depending on the primary objective—such as maximizing carbon sequestration or protecting threatened species—and within the boundaries of budget limitations, different spatial priorities have been identified at global and regional scales. Funding mechanisms to support such work comprise public sources, philanthropy, and the private sector, including the sale of carbon and biodiversity credits. However, effectively exploring trade‐offs among restoration objectives and estimating the price of biodiversity and carbon credits to design financially viable projects remains scientifically challenging. Here we harness the power of artificial intelligence implemented in the software CAPTAIN to identify spatial priorities for ecological restoration that maximize multiple objectives at once and to allow a robust evaluation of biodiversity and climate outcomes. We find through a series of simulations that even low‐to‐moderate consideration of biodiversity in the design of restoration projects leads to the selection of restored areas that disproportionately improve the conservation of threatened species, while the carbon captured is only slightly reduced. We propose the bundling of biodiversity and carbon credits to support restoration efforts even in areas previously excluded for economic reasons. Applying our methodology to plant diversity in the Atlantic Forest of eastern South America, one of the most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems globally, we demonstrate its potential to guide restoration and to quantify trade‐offs between multiple optimization scenarios. Our study provides a robust, scalable method to maximize the joint benefits of ecological restoration for climate and nature.

articles.title: Is the US Warming Hole a Moist‐Enthalpy Hole? Soil‐Moisture Trends Organize Dry and Moist Heat Across CONUS
articles.titleEn: Is the US Warming Hole a Moist‐Enthalpy Hole? Soil‐Moisture Trends Organize Dry and Moist Heat Across CONUS
articles.abstract: The United States (US) summer warming hole, marked by muted warming or cooling in maximum dry‐bulb temperature ( T max ) across parts of the central and southeastern US, is a regional exception to broader warming. However, T max does not capture atmospheric total heat content when humidity changes simultaneously. Using ERA5 reanalysis from 1950 to 2020, we examine summer trends in T max , maximum wet‐bulb temperature ( T w ,max ), and maximum equivalent temperature ( T e ,max ) across the contiguous US (CONUS). The dry‐bulb warming hole strengthens from June to August, yet humidity‐sensitive metrics show sustained increases across many of the same areas. Decomposing T e into temperature and humidity contributions shows that rising specific humidity offsets or exceeds weak or negative T max trends throughout much of the warming hole region. In the moistening core of the region, a latent heat contribution of order +0.5°C decade −1 accompanies near‐zero dry‐bulb trends. This opposition between sensible and latent contributions makes the warming hole fundamentally metric‐dependent. Moist‐heat amplification co‐occurs with wetting soil moisture, rising latent heat flux, and shallower boundary layers, whereas the most strongly drying regions show boundary‐layer deepening and a negative humidity contribution. The US warming hole thus reflects a shift in heat exposure from sensible toward latent forms, linking regional heat‐risk assessment to humidity, soil moisture, and boundary‐layer processes.

articles.title: Projected Climate Change Impacts on Deep‐Sea Corals of the Red Sea
articles.titleEn: Projected Climate Change Impacts on Deep‐Sea Corals of the Red Sea
articles.abstract: Ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation, among other co‐occurring factors, are shifting species ranges throughout the marine environment. Mesophotic and deep corals are understudied in their response to climate changes, particularly in the Red Sea, which has relatively high temperatures and salinities and is projected to undergo major changes in the future, with little assessment of the impacts to date. Ecological niche modelling can be used to explain the known distribution of a species, predict its current range, and estimate future range shift under changing ocean scenarios. Here, we estimate the area of suitable habitat for four mesophotic and deep‐sea corals ( Acanthogorgia spp., Stylaster tritoni, Bathypathes thermophila , and Madracis interjecta ) across the whole Red Sea under present conditions and under different scenarios of future environmental changes (years 2090–2100). We found variations in the responses of these corals, but two of the four taxa are projected to lose significant amounts of their current habitats, while the other two lose a smaller portion. In particular, the scleractinian coral M. interjecta is likely to lose the largest proportion of its habitat, while the black coral B. thermophila may experience the least change. Deeper areas may become suitable for these corals, but colonisation will depend on their ability to disperse. We also assessed the potential biodiversity hotspots both now and in the future, finding the northern Red Sea to be one ecologically important area. These results enable marine spatial planning in support of an effective long‐term conservation action to protect these important habitats.

articles.title: Deadwood Mitigates Declines in Soil Food‐Web Energy Fluxes in Canopy Gaps
articles.titleEn: Deadwood Mitigates Declines in Soil Food‐Web Energy Fluxes in Canopy Gaps
articles.abstract: Across forests worldwide, frequent climate extremes and intensified timber harvest are reshaping forest structure by increasing tree mortality and canopy opening, threatening terrestrial biodiversity and ecosystem sustainability. In unmanaged forests, natural disturbances create canopy gaps and leave substantial deadwood on site, whereas timber harvesting creates gaps through the removal of living trees, thereby limiting the accumulation of deadwood. However, how these disturbances and management practices affect ecosystem functioning, especially of the belowground system, remains little understood. Here, we reconstructed 116 soil animal food webs in a full‐factorial experiment manipulating forest gaps and deadwood addition. We quantified energy fluxes of soil food webs as an integrative measure of belowground ecosystem functioning and investigated their network architecture 2 years after establishment of the experiment. Forest gaps reduced total food web energy fluxes by 13.4%, decreased network connectance, and shifted energy flow towards the bacteria‐dominated “fast” channel, indicating simplified soil food webs, impaired soil functioning, and reduced energy retention belowground. However, compared to gaps without deadwood, the presence of deadwood in gaps increased total energy flux by 37.4%, primarily through enhanced fungivory and wood‐feeding pathways, and restored network connectance and cycling rates to levels comparable to those in closed‐canopy forests. Our results demonstrate that deadwood acts as a key structural component that mitigates the detrimental effects of canopy gap formation on belowground ecosystem functioning, underscoring deadwood retention after timber harvest as a practical strategy to safeguard soil functioning in a more disturbance‐prone future.

articles.title: The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
articles.titleEn: The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
articles.abstract: Carbon removal markets lack a standardized, quantitative measure of permanence risk. Inspired by value at risk in financial markets, we propose carbon at risk (CaR): a probabilistic measure of the shortfall between contracted removals and realized storage at a given confidence level and time horizon. We calibrate CaR in two proof-of-concept applications: forest carbon, where Monte Carlo simulations driven by satellite fire data yield a single-project 95% CaR of more than 70% over 200 years for California, and geological storage, where simulations using the Storage Security Calculator show that the 95% CaR ranges from 0.15% (well-regulated offshore) to 17% (poorly regulated onshore). Combining technologies in a portfolio can help manage tail risk cost-effectively. The minimum cost of meeting a permanence target depends on the magnitude and correlation structure of key risk factors. CaR provides a technology-agnostic basis for risk-calibrated buffer sizing, insurance pricing and reserve-fund design, over both policy- and climate-relevant horizons.

articles.title: Elevated early Eocene atmospheric CO2 tied to reduced Southern Ocean biological pump efficiency
articles.titleEn: Elevated early Eocene atmospheric CO2 tied to reduced Southern Ocean biological pump efficiency
articles.abstract: The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum (53 to 49 million years ago) was an interval in Earth’s history when reconstructed temperatures and atmospheric CO 2 concentrations were among the highest of the Cenozoic Era (that is, the last 66 million years). The causes of the high CO 2 levels remain unclear. CO 2 changes over recent ice age cycles appear to be largely controlled by the biologically mediated build-up and release of carbon from the Southern Ocean, a process that might have also played a role earlier in the Cenozoic. Here we test this possibility with foraminifera-bound nitrogen isotope measurements. Our data show higher surface nitrate concentrations in the Southern Ocean, and thus a more inefficient biological sequestration of carbon during peak Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. The associated transfer of CO 2 from the deep ocean to the atmosphere would have been amplified by the low seawater buffering capacity of the Eocene, due to the lower pH and high Ca ion concentration. Previously proposed low silicate rock weatherability during the Eocene may have weakened the weathering thermostat, allowing the reconstructed change in biological pump efficiency in the Southern Ocean to explain at least half of the atmospheric CO 2 increase observed during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

articles.title: Daily global sea surface ageostrophic current dataset from 1993–2023 via physics-informed deep learning
articles.titleEn: Daily global sea surface ageostrophic current dataset from 1993–2023 via physics-informed deep learning
articles.abstract: Surface ocean circulation shapes climate, air–sea exchange, and the transport of heat, carbon, and other tracers, yet most long-term global datasets rely primarily on geostrophic balance and therefore miss important ageostrophic motions. Here, we reconstruct global daily sea surface circulation at 0.25° resolution from 1993 to 2023 using a physics-informed framework that integrates satellite altimetry with momentum constraints from geostrophic balance, wind stress, and nonlinear advection (Cui, 2026; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19966716). The resulting dataset is dynamically consistent, with a mean momentum balance error below 1.5 %, and reduces the median velocity error against independent mooring observations across the tropical Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans to 0.07 m s −1 , compared with 0.20 m s −1 for geostrophic currents and 0.10 m s −1 for Ekman corrected currents. We show that geostrophic flow sets the large-scale circulation, whereas Ekman and nonlinear contributions are smaller but comparable in magnitude to each other. Although nonlinear advection contributes little to relative vorticity, it strongly shapes surface divergence and the fine scale structure of eddy kinetic energy. Our results show that nonlinear ageostrophic flow is an essential component of global surface circulation and that neglecting it limits our ability to resolve surface transport and variability on climatically relevant scales.

articles.title: Exploring Air–Sea Interactions in a Regional Weakly Coupled Data Assimilation System: An Observing System Experiment for the 2023 Indian Ocean Monsoon and Cyclone Biparjoy
articles.titleEn: Exploring Air–Sea Interactions in a Regional Weakly Coupled Data Assimilation System: An Observing System Experiment for the 2023 Indian Ocean Monsoon and Cyclone Biparjoy
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: We examined air–sea interactions in a weakly coupled ocean–atmosphere data assimilation (DA) system by performing an observing system experiment (OSE). The OSE is performed for the Arabian Sea monsoon onset event in 2023, which also coincides with the passage of the tropical cyclone Biparjoy. Results show that assimilating both oceanic and atmospheric data produces a better forecast of the ocean–atmosphere state (fit to the assimilated data) than either experiment assimilating only oceanic or atmospheric data. This indicates that the coupled system provides more consistent initial conditions, yielding more balanced oceanic and atmospheric states when assimilating all the data. However, we found that assimilating only atmospheric data improves both the ocean and atmosphere state forecasts, whereas assimilating only oceanic data improves the ocean state forecasts but degrades the atmospheric state forecasts, when compared with the free run (coupled model simulation without assimilating any data). We found that this counterintuitive model performance is due to the systematic misrepresentation of air–sea exchanges. First, errors in the cyclone path increase when atmospheric data are not assimilated. Then, assimilation of sea surface temperature (SST) leads to a warmer SST below the misplaced cyclone (with cyclone path offset of about 200 km relative to IBTrACS data), resulting in increased cyclone intensity. This misrepresentation of air–sea exchanges not only occurs during the cyclone passage but also persists throughout the early monsoon season. Since errors in one component can affect the other and result in positive feedback, leading to error growth, this study highlights an interesting effect on weakly coupled ocean–atmosphere DA systems when atmospheric data are unavailable or limited in space and time, particularly during high‐impact atmospheric events such as tropical cyclones.

articles.title: Improvement of a Regional Multiscale NLS‐4DVar Assimilation System Based on the CWRF‐CoLM Coupled Model
articles.titleEn: Improvement of a Regional Multiscale NLS‐4DVar Assimilation System Based on the CWRF‐CoLM Coupled Model
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Ensemble perturbations in 4DEnVar‐type methods are pulled in two directions at once: estimating a reliable background‐error covariance (BEC) calls for perturbations large enough to sample real error structure, while a valid tangent‐linear (TL) approximation calls for perturbations small enough to stay near‐linear. This study resolves this conflict by introducing a shrinkage factor () into a multigrid NLS‐4DVar framework, decoupling the perturbation scale used for BEC estimation from that used for TL approximation. An independent finite‐difference test verifies this decoupling, showing that TL accuracy is governed by a trade‐off between nonlinear truncation error and numerical error. Based on this framework, an improved Regional Multiscale Nonlinear Least Squares (NLS) 4DVar Data Assimilation System was developed based on the CWRF‐CoLM coupled model. A 1‐month cycling assimilation experiment (July 2021) shows that the new scheme (DA2) outperforms the original (DA1): analysis RMSE and bias are reduced for U / V winds, T , and QVAPOR, 3‐day forecast RMSE improves broadly, and the 24‐hr precipitation threat score at moderate‐to‐heavy rainfall thresholds is notably higher, which is consistent with a preferential benefit for strongly nonlinear moisture and convective processes. Although only atmospheric observations are assimilated, land‐surface forecasts (2‐m temperature, 2‐m humidity, soil moisture) also improve indirectly, driven by a more accurate initial moisture field and better‐represented land‐atmosphere coupling. Beyond its practical performance, this decoupling strategy completes a previously unverified aspect of the NLS‐4DVar formulation and offers a generalizable approach for mitigating nonlinear errors in ensemble‐based variational assimilation.

articles.title: Machine Learning‐Based Representation of Model Error and Observation Error With Estimated Cross‐Correlation in Data Assimilation
articles.titleEn: Machine Learning‐Based Representation of Model Error and Observation Error With Estimated Cross‐Correlation in Data Assimilation
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: The current study presents machine learning (ML)‐based schemes that independently represent model error and observation error during data assimilation. The Model Error ML scheme (MLME) uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to produce flow‐dependent model corrections. The Observation Error ML scheme (MLOE) also uses the GAN to adaptively estimate the observation error covariance matrix. Furthermore, a generalized formulation (CorrFOE) is derived to incorporate the often‐neglected cross‐correlations between forecast and observation errors. The proposed schemes are rigorously evaluated via twin experiments with the Lorenz III model. Results show that the ML‐based schemes reduce the root‐mean‐square error (RMSE) of analyses relative to the control and, for model error, relative to the additive‐noise baseline. Additionally, the MLME scheme is particularly effective at recovering small‐scale structures. Crucially, the synergistic combination of both ML schemes with the explicit inclusion of cross‐correlation between forecast and observation errors produces the most accurate analyses. The added computational costs for MLME, MLOE and CorrFOE are moderate, confirming their operational potential.

articles.title: Physics‐Informed Neural Networks as Differentiable Surrogates for 4D‐Variational Data Assimilation
articles.titleEn: Physics‐Informed Neural Networks as Differentiable Surrogates for 4D‐Variational Data Assimilation
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Biogeochemical forecasting requires state estimation methods that accommodate sparse observations, nonlinear dynamics, and discontinuous ecological processes. Four‐dimensional variational data assimilation addresses this challenge but depends on tangent‐linear and adjoint models that are costly to derive and maintain alongside evolving forward codes, and that are not defined where biogeochemical formulations are non‐differentiable. We propose a framework in which a physics‐informed neural network (PINN) replaces the traditional numerical model and its linearizations, remaining differentiable through automatic differentiation while embedding simplified governing equations as structural guardrails and computing the forward, tangent‐linear, and adjoint operators simultaneously from a single computational graph. Applied to nitrate‐phytoplankton‐zooplankton dynamics as a controlled testbed, our approach achieves an approximately six‐fold speedup over traditional numerical models in twin experiments while maintaining comparable state estimation accuracy across observation sampling scenarios. Jacobian analysis shows that the learned sensitivities are consistent with the embedded ecological relationships where these agree with the data, while departing where simplified formulations prove inadequate. This framework demonstrates that PINN‐based surrogates can maintain dynamical consistency in variational data assimilation while reducing implementation burden, offering a path toward more flexible and maintainable forecasting systems for increasingly complex biogeochemical models.

articles.title: New Representation of Sea Ice Salt Dynamics in NEMO‐SI 3 v5: Evaluation and Impacts
articles.titleEn: New Representation of Sea Ice Salt Dynamics in NEMO‐SI 3 v5: Evaluation and Impacts
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Although many large‐scale sea ice models now represent salt dynamics, few studies have evaluated them, and uncertainty remains regarding key parameterization choices. Here, we conduct global 1° ocean–ice simulations with NEMO‐SI 3 v5, forced by climatological atmospheric data, tuned to the salinity–thickness relationship, and evaluated against more than 1,400 ice cores. Simulations investigate (a) the treatment of vertical ice salinity variations (diagnostic vs. prognostic), (b) gravity drainage physics (brine fraction‐based vs. Rayleigh number‐based), and (c) key parameter values. On average, ice salinity is simulated within 0.1 g/kg (Arctic) and 0.7 g/kg (Antarctic) of observations, capturing large‐scale features including the Arctic–Antarctic contrast, seasonality, vertical profile, and the salinity–thickness relationship. Using a high value for the new ice liquid fraction parameter is critical for simulating high salinity in the thin ice range. Vertically‐resolved salt dynamics generally outperform the diagnostic approach, consistently across hemispheres, seasons, depth and thickness. Brine fraction‐based and Rayleigh number‐based parameterizations of gravity drainage produce different salinity fields, both through direct effects and interactions with melt ponds. However, limited observational constraints on measurement biases prevent firm conclusions on which approach performs best. Uncertainties in ice salinity are generally larger in the Antarctic than in the Arctic. While salt dynamics strongly affect sea ice mass and salt budget terms, they affect sea ice volume moderately, and have little effect on ocean salinity due to compensating effects.

articles.title: An Unstructured Voronoi Mesh Framework for Large‐Scale Hydrologic and Land Surface Models
articles.titleEn: An Unstructured Voronoi Mesh Framework for Large‐Scale Hydrologic and Land Surface Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Accurate representation of river networks and land surface heterogeneity is crucial for improving the performance of continental‐to‐global hydrologic and land surface models. Traditional approaches rely on either coarse‐resolution grids, which may oversimplify complex terrain and limit the accurate representation of key processes, or computationally demanding full‐domain high‐resolution meshes. This study expands upon our previous research on unstructured mesh‐based hydrologic modeling by introducing a novel framework for generating Hydrologic Refined Meshes (HRMs). This framework seamlessly integrates crucial land surface features, including river networks, watershed boundaries, and lake boundaries, into the mesh generation process. The HRM framework provides a generalized, feature‐driven workflow for strategic mesh refinement; here, we implement it within the Model for Prediction Across Scales architecture, leveraging its Centroidal Voronoi Tessellations properties and dual‐grid topology. The resulting variable‐resolution (4–50 km) Voronoi mesh accurately captures these features, demonstrating significant advantages in representing land surface heterogeneity. For instance, the mesh effectively captures surface elevation, resolving most key landscape features despite using nearly half the cell count. River networks are accurately represented by high‐resolution cells aligned along their courses, resulting in a conceptual network that deviates by only approximately on average from the true river network. We demonstrate the applicability of this framework and evaluate the generated mesh using several key variables, including surface elevation and river networks.

articles.title: Past and future projected radiative effects from irrigation
articles.titleEn: Past and future projected radiative effects from irrigation
articles.abstract: Irrigation is the most dominant freshwater use practice on Earth, yet its effect on the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiative budget remains uncertain because past estimates have relied on idealised experiments or single-model frameworks. Here, we use historical simulations (1902–2014) from the Irrigation Model Intercomparison Project (IRRMIP) to provide the first multi-model quantification of irrigation-induced effective radiative forcing (ERF), defined as the change in net TOA radiative flux including rapid atmospheric adjustments. Across seven Earth system models, under prescribed sea surface temperatures (SST), the global multi-model mean (MMM) irrigation-induced ERF is positive but small (∼ 0.023 W m −2 ). While the global signal is small, it masks regional heterogeneity: South Asia and West Central Asia exhibit higher positive ERF (∼0.23 W m −2 ), with spatial maps revealing coherent forcing hotspots of up to +5 W m −2 over the Indo-Gangetic Plain that are consistent across all models, while East Asia shows negative ERF (∼-0.03 W m −2 ). The clear-sky ERF is greater than the all-sky ERF in most of the regions, indicating that cloud adjustments following irrigation may exert a negative contribution to the ERF. Correlations between historical irrigation ERF variability and its potential drivers suggest that reduced outgoing longwave radiation is the dominant control at the global scale, as well as in South Asia and West Central Asia, while near-surface temperature, precipitable water, albedo, and cloud cover contribute with substantial regional and inter-model variability. We additionally examine future changes in net TOA radiation imbalance (Δ R n,TOA ) from a fully coupled CMIP-style model (SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0, 2015–2070) to assess whether the historical ERF pattern persists under future irrigation. The global mean Δ R n,TOA is more positive under the high irrigation demand pathway (SSP3-7.0) than under SSP1-2.6, consistent with projected differences in irrigation expansion between scenarios. These results demonstrate that irrigation's radiative influence, while small in the global mean, is regionally substantial and scenario-dependent, with implications for the attribution of regional climate change and for the design of land-based mitigation trajectories.

articles.titleEn: Towards improved integration of hydrological uncertainty and hydraulic model sensitivity in flood hazard mapping
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The study presents a novel framework for integrating hydrological uncertainties and the related sensitivity of the hydrodynamic modelling results into flood hazard mapping. Uncertainties in flood frequency analysis (FFA), including anticipated impact of climate change and sensitivity to channel and floodplain roughness, were examined through selected scenario ensembles. The study area is the lower Vipava river, a transboundary catchment shared between Slovenia and Italy with variable floodplain topography. Sensitivity analysis revealed that uncertainty in FFA and river channel roughness significantly influenced the inundation spatial extent and inundation depth, the impact of floodplain roughness appears to be limited. The analysis shows that natural successional changes in river channel roughness substantially impact the results of a 10 year return period (RP) event, increasing flood extent by 45 %. The increase in inundated areas is less pronounced for 100 and 500 year RP floods, with increases of 15 % and 11 %, respectively. The weighted exceedance probability of inundation (WEPI) based on scenario ensembles provided an informative identification of areas most susceptible to potential changes in flood hazard. Our results highlight the value of targeted scenario ensembles that incorporate FFA uncertainty and hydraulic roughness sensitivity, thereby producing more informative flood hazard mapping that can complement deterministic mapping approaches and support more adaptive future land use planning.

articles.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
articles.titleEn: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
articles.abstract: Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age 1–3 . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested 4 , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts 5–8 . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory 9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

articles.title: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.titleEn: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.abstract: Groundwater stores a third of all global freshwater and supports water supply, irrigation and ecosystems across the world. As such, groundwater drought can have wide-reaching financial, social and environmental impacts, particularly when drought events are prolonged or multi-year. Although recent work has made significant progress in understanding the drivers and patterns of multi-year meteorological droughts, we do not know how this signal translates into multi-year groundwater drought, where subsurface processes, anthropogenic influences and abstractions can alter the meteorological signal. This is particularly true at the global-scale, where a major barrier to understanding large-scale groundwater drought dynamics is the difficulty of obtaining consistent and comprehensive groundwater data. In this research, we use a new global hyper-resolution (∼1 km) groundwater dataset to investigate the global patterns and drivers of groundwater drought from 1960–2019, with a specific focus on multi-year events. We start by characterizing the propagation of meteorological (represented by SPEI-12) to groundwater drought, evaluating how and to what extent the sub-surface plays a role in modulating the meteorological drought signal. Subsequently, we define three global groundwater response types that provide a framework for understanding the processes and geo-physical drivers of normal versus multi-year groundwater droughts. We find that 35 % of global groundwater grid cells have an average groundwater drought duration which is multi-year. In 83 % of these locations, the subsurface extends the meteorological drought signal, whereas in the remaining 17 %, groundwater drought duration appears to be primarily driven by meteorological anomalies. Our analysis offers new insights into global-scale drought exposure by identifying regions which have been most vulnerable to multi-year groundwater drought in the past, as well as those which might be more vulnerable in the future. Importantly, our typology also highlights areas where multi-year groundwater droughts can be anticipated based on meteorological drought anomalies and can therefore inform strategies for managing and mitigating future water scarcity risks.

articles.title: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.titleEn: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.abstract: Terrestrial vegetation regulates global carbon cycling and climate through responses to water availability. Yet, it remains unclear whether soil moisture (SM) or atmospheric dryness (vapour pressure deficit, VPD) dominates vegetation responses and, more critically, how their relative influence changes over time, limiting predictions of ecosystem–climate feedback under warming. Here we analyse satellite-derived vegetation variability over the past four decades using an explainable artificial intelligence framework that disentangles nonlinear hydroclimatic driver contributions. We show SM dominates vegetation variability in most regions. However, VPD influence has strengthened while SM influence has weakened over time. These changes highlight an asymmetric transition with more SM-dominated ecosystems shifting towards increasing VPD control than vice versa. Changes in the mean and variability of SM and VPD drive this transition by altering plant water-stress responses. Continued warming will probably intensify this pattern as rising VPD and more frequent extreme events strengthen atmospheric constraints on vegetation.

articles.title: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.titleEn: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.abstract: Several methods have been proposed and used to refine estimates of future climate change based on combined output from comprehensive climate models. While previously the so-called model democracy approach was used to combine model outputs, where every model is given equal weight, it is now widely accepted that using model weights that account for model performance and model independence is necessary to obtain more reliable results. However, most existing approaches rely, implicitly or explicitly, on a similar statistical basis, while describing things in different ways. Here we distinguish between approaches that are based on the performance of individual models (individual performance weighting) and approaches that are based on the performance of the weighted ensemble as a whole (ensemble performance weighting). At the same time, we formulate both in probabilistic Bayesian terms to make their application and comparison straightforward. Using simple constructed examples, we demonstrate that the ensemble performance weighting approach implicitly accounts for co-dependencies among models, which arguably makes the computation of independence weights for the purpose of model weighting obsolete. We also show that a set of weighted models within the ensemble weighting approach will naturally tend to artificially reduce uncertainty and that this is strongly influenced by the choice of the prior distribution over weight vectors. The distinction between individual and ensemble performance weighting is both methodological and conceptual. Formulating both approaches in general probabilistic Bayesian terms as done here, can serve as a common basis for future developments with regard to ensemble model weighting in Earth system science. The discussed concepts are generally applicable across domains and are thus possibly relevant for other modeling communities as well.

articles.title: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
articles.titleEn: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
articles.abstract: Nuclear conflicts could ignite intense fires that inject considerable amounts of black carbon (BC) into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere, with the potential to disrupt global climate. While uncertainties in the BC injection remain large, relatively few modeling studies have explored the climatic response to more limited nuclear exchange between major nuclear powers. Here, we investigate the climate response to a set of relatively limited-forcing scenarios (12 to 24 Tg BC) for nuclear exchanges between the United States and Russia. This corresponds to one-tenth to one-fifth of the forcing strength of typically considered. We use the Canadian Earth System Model version 5, an independent contributor to the worldwide set of Earth System Models that has not been explored previously in this application. Consistent with previous work, decreased downwelling shortwave radiation at the surface drives prolonged surface cooling. Unexpectedly, however, a transient surface warming develops in the first boreal summer following a boreal-winter injection, linked to reduced cooling via net longwave and turbulent fluxes. The transient warming is most pronounced for the lowest forcing cases. Precipitation, which decreases even while the surface warms, is found to be controlled by stabilizing, top-heavy warming. Multi-model assessment of these relatively limited-forcing cases is warranted given their potential impacts.

articles.title: Benchmarking conditioners in Liang–Kleeman Information Flow: application to land–atmosphere interactions in humid forests
articles.titleEn: Benchmarking conditioners in Liang–Kleeman Information Flow: application to land–atmosphere interactions in humid forests
articles.abstract: The Liang–Kleeman Information Flow (LKIF) framework has been increasingly used to identify causality in Earth–system dynamics in recent years. Yet, uncertainties remain regarding how the causal graph changes when mediators and confounders (conditioners) are introduced, i.e., divergence between the bivariate and conditioned forms. A controlled synthetic experiment shows that LKIF preserves correct causal directions under hidden confounding, while differences between bivariate and multivariate estimates still occur. We characterize these differences using time-varying LKIF and introduce several quantifiers, including Conditioner Dominance Index, Moderation Gain, Conditioning Pressure, and Convergence Rate, to evaluate the contributions of conditioners. This is illustrated in an application to soil moisture (SM) and vapor pressure deficit (VPD) couplings with vegetation (leaf area index (LAI) and gross primary productivity (GPP)) in humid forest regions of Southeast China and the Amazon Basin, using satellite-derived and reanalysis data over 1981–2018. We find that the influence of SM on LAI remains consistently stable and shows little sensitivity to the selected conditioners, whereas its influence on GPP and that of VPD on vegetation exhibit substantial divergence between bivariate and multivariate estimates. This divergence peaks under compound dry–hot conditions, with VPD and temperature emerging as dominant conditioners. These results demonstrate that bivariate and multivariate LKIF can yield markedly different conclusions across time and space, especially under compound environmental stress. More importantly, even for the same variables in a causal graph, the same conditioners can affect the temporal evolution of the causal relationships very differently at different locations. This highlights how stationary assumptions may oversimplify causal structure by masking relevant temporal transitions, particularly under compound environmental stress.

articles.title: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.titleEn: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.abstract: The Congo Basin in Central Africa remains one of the few regions globally where the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has neither assessed changes in hot extremes and extreme precipitation since the 1950s nor attributed such changes to anthropogenic influences, primarily due to the sparsity of in situ observational data. Although extensive daily weather records exist, spanning from the 1900s to the early 2000s and covering numerous stations across the basin, the majority of these remain archived on paper, limiting their accessibility for climate analysis. Here we present and analyse over 1 million temperature and precipitation observations from 37 weather stations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which have until now been unavailable to the research community. To produce this dataset, we first digitized (imaged) 9885 paper sheets stored in local archives during two dedicated field campaigns. We subsequently apply an improved version of the MeteoSaver software (version 1.1) to transcribe the imaged sheets, yielding daily time series of maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, precipitation, as well as dry bulb and wet bulb temperatures measured at three times per day (06:00, 15:00, and 18:00 local time). After quality control, analysis of multi-decadal temperature data across the basin reveals a consistent and accelerating warming signal since the 1960s, characterized by a warming shift in the distribution of daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures with each successive decade. Median trends across 21 of the 37 stations with sufficient data availability are 0.22, 0.10, and 0.15 °C per decade for daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, respectively, corresponding to approximately 0.7, 0.3, and 0.5 °C of warming during the 1961–1990 period. We further find an increasing frequency of hot extremes and a decreasing frequency of cold extremes with each successive decade, with the most recent decade exhibiting nearly twice as many hot days per year and fewer cold days compared to the earliest decade. Analysis of precipitation at three stations with sufficient data indicates an increased frequency of heavy precipitation events at two stations and no substantial change at the third; however, limited spatial coverage due to data availability restricts broader conclusions for the DRC. Overall, this analysis of rescued weather data from Central Africa highlights the urgent need to close the knowledge gap on climate trends in the Congo Basin, one of the world's most data-sparse yet climatically significant regions.

articles.title: Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
articles.titleEn: Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
articles.abstract: It is not really questioned today that climate can be described in theory by an ensemble of trajectories differing in their initial conditions, which is then translated to numerical ensembles in climate models. It is also widely accepted that any evolution observed within a few decades after initialization is not yet relevant to climate. Evolution at a later stage, instead, is then used to characterize climate and its change, under the implicit assumption that slower processes do not considerably contribute to differences between ensemble members, allowing internal variability of climate to be identified with these differences. However, a careful justification for this practice is as yet lacking. In particular, a definition of climate in support of this practice is outstanding, including the identification of the kind of time scales at play through providing an argumentation for their relevance. Our study aims at filling this gap. After pointing out that the most important criterion for a definition of climate is the uniqueness of the probability measure on which the definition relies, we first recall the naive proposal to represent such a probability measure by the distribution of ensemble members that has, loosely speaking, converged to the natural probability measure of the so-called snapshot or pullback attractor of the dynamics. We then consider the time scales of convergence and refine the proposal by taking a probability measure that is conditional on the (possibly time-evolving) state of modes characterized by convergence time scales longer than the horizon of a particular study. We design an ensemble simulation initialization scheme for studying convergence time scales and uniqueness of ensembles in Earth system models.
articles.abstractEn: It is not really questioned today that climate can be described in theory by an ensemble of trajectories differing in their initial conditions, which is then translated to numerical ensembles in climate models. It is also widely accepted that any evolution observed within a few decades after initialization is not yet relevant to climate. Evolution at a later stage, instead, is then used to characterize climate and its change, under the implicit assumption that slower processes do not considerably contribute to differences between ensemble members, allowing internal variability of climate to be identified with these differences. However, a careful justification for this practice is as yet lacking. In particular, a definition of climate in support of this practice is outstanding, including the identification of the kind of time scales at play through providing an argumentation for their relevance. Our study aims at filling this gap. After pointing out that the most important criterion for a definition of climate is the uniqueness of the probability measure on which the definition relies, we first recall the naive proposal to represent such a probability measure by the distribution of ensemble members that has, loosely speaking, converged to the natural probability measure of the so-called snapshot or pullback attractor of the dynamics. We then consider the time scales of convergence and refine the proposal by taking a probability measure that is conditional on the (possibly time-evolving) state of modes characterized by convergence time scales longer than the horizon of a particular study. We design an ensemble simulation initialization scheme for studying convergence time scales and uniqueness of ensembles in Earth system models.

articles.title: Impacts of simulated coastal ocean alkalinity enhancement on the seasonal carbon cycle in European waters under a low- and a high-emission scenario
articles.titleEn: Impacts of simulated coastal ocean alkalinity enhancement on the seasonal carbon cycle in European waters under a low- and a high-emission scenario
articles.abstract: One potentially scalable method to remove CO 2 from the air is ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), which works to lower the ocean's CO 2 partial pressure ( p CO 2 ) and accelerate CO 2 sequestration and durable storage. This study explores how OAE might affect the seasonal carbon cycle, which plays a key role in the ocean's annual CO 2 uptake. By analysing Earth System Model simulations of OAE implemented continuously at the European coastline under low and high emissions, it was found that: (a) due to surface alkalinity retention, OAE reduces ocean p CO 2 most strongly in summer, turning the region into a year-round carbon sink; (b) the strongest air-sea CO 2 uptake enhancement takes place in winter; (c) the ocean's carbon sink is increased more strongly in SSP3-7.0 than in SSP1-2.6 due to a lower buffering capacity.
